findings.ca_experience: The CA clicks Post on the Depreciation tab. The Dr Depreciation Expense / Cr Accumulated Depreciation journal lands on the ledger, then the request errors. findings.title: The default "Schedule II" WDV rates are not Schedule II rates — a computer depreciates at half the correct rate
findings.evidence: routers/fixed_assets.py:41-51 `_DEFAULT_WDV_RATES` = {Plant & Machinery 15.33, Furniture & Fixtures 10.00, Computer & IT Equipment 31.67, Office Equipment 13.91, Vehicles 25.89, Building 5.00, Intangibles 25.00, Other 15.33}, under a comment claiming "Companies Act 2013 Schedule II". apps/web/app/clients/[id]/fixed-assets/page.tsx:64-74 duplicates the identical table and the form labels it "Companies Act 2013 Sch II rate pre-filled for selected category" (line 428). Schedule II Part C prescribes USEFUL LIVES, from which the WDV rate is R = 1 − (residual/cost)^(1/n); at the 5% residual cap in Part C's notes: n=3 (end-user computers) → 63.16%, n=6 (servers/networks) → 39.30%, n=5 (office equipment) → 45.07%, n=10 (furniture & fittings) → 25.89%, n=15 (general plant & machinery) → 18.10%, n=8 (motor cars) → 31.23%, n=60/30 (buildings RCC/non-RCC) → 4.87%/9.50%. None of the eight non-zero table entries matches its category's Part C life; several are the OLD Companies Act 1956 Schedule XIV rates (13.91% = general P&M single shift), and the mapping is scrambled — 13.91% corresponds to a 20-year life and is assigned to Office Equipment, whose Part C life is 5 years.
findings.ca_experience: A ₹1,00,000 laptop charges ₹31,670 in year one instead of ~₹63,160. Every asset created without the CA overriding the rate is depreciated at the wrong rate for its whole life: profit is overstated, net block is overstated, and the signed balance sheet and P&L are wrong by a material amount for any client with a real asset base. Because the UI states the rate is Schedule II, the CA has no reason to check it.
findings.market_standard: Dedicated Schedule II tools (and every Companies Act depreciation utility a CA uses) ask for the USEFUL LIFE and the residual %, derive the WDV rate, and fully write the asset down to residual at the end of that life. Rates are never typed as a free number labelled Schedule II.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the rate table with a Schedule II Part C useful-life table (a real statutory table, versioned like the other registries in domain/), store `useful_life_years` + `residual_percent` per asset, and DERIVE the WDV rate. Put it in a domain module so the frontend reads it from the backend instead of holding a second copy. Until then, remove the 'Schedule II' label from both the code comment and the UI, because it is the label that stops anyone checking.

findings.title: The Depreciation tab recomputes the annual charge in TypeScript with the exact bug the backend fixed in #232
findings.evidence: apps/web/app/clients/[id]/fixed-assets/page.tsx:517-528 `annualDepn()` computes `wdv = cost − accumulated` then, for WDV, `Math.floor(wdv * rate / 100)` — i.e. from the LIVE accumulated depreciation. routers/fixed_assets.py:100-140 `_annual_depreciation_for_period` exists precisely because that is wrong: it caches the opening-of-FY accumulated depreciation (`depreciation_fy_start_accum_paise`, migration 239) so the annual figure is fixed for the year. findings.ca_experience: On 1 April the tab says the annual charge is ₹31,670. By January, after nine monthly postings, the same asset's tile says ~₹25,000 — the number visibly shrinks each month, and the 'Monthly Depn' column the CA reads before clicking Post is not the amount that gets posted. findings.market_standard: A depreciation schedule is computed once, server-side, per financial year and displayed identically wherever it appears.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete `annualDepn` and render `/api/fixed-assets/depreciation-schedule`, which already returns annual_depreciation_paise and monthly_depreciation_paise per asset. findings.title: Depreciation is monthly-only with no catch-up, and a missed month can never be posted
findings.evidence: routers/fixed_assets.py:302 charges `monthly = floor(annual/12)` for exactly one month per call. Line 279: `if asset.get("depreciation_posted_through") and asset["depreciation_posted_through"] >= period: raise 409`. There is no annual mode, no from/to range, and no job — grep of jobs/*.py for 'deprec' returns nothing. The only bulk path is the browser loop at apps/web/app/clients/[id]/fixed-assets/page.tsx:507-513, one HTTP request per asset for ONE month, with every error swallowed at line 502.
findings.ca_experience: Two realistic failures. (a) A CA who does the books once a year opens the client in March, clicks 'Post All for Period' for 2027-03, and gets one twelfth of the year's depreciation in the P&L — the register and the accounts are understated by 11/12 of the charge and nothing says so. (b) A CA who posted April–August, skipped September while the client was late with data, then posted October, can never go back: October set posted_through, so September is refused with a 409 forever and that month's depreciation is permanently missing.
findings.market_standard: Every FA module has a depreciation RUN for a period range that computes the charge for all assets from the last posted date to the run date, and reports what it posted per asset. Winman and Zoho both run it annually or for a chosen range; none requires twelve clicks per asset per year.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `POST /api/fixed-assets/run-depreciation` taking client_id and a from/to period range, iterating each asset's unposted months server-side in one transaction and returning a per-asset result; make the 409 apply per-period rather than as a high-water mark so gaps can be filled. Keep the per-asset endpoint for corrections.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Depreciation posts exactly one month per call, with no range/annual mode and no catch-up, and routers/fixed_assets.py:279 makes depreciation_posted_through a permanent high-water mark: posting October after August silently charges one month rather than two, and September is then refused with a 409 forever. The bulk path is a browser for-loop (apps/web/app/clients/[id]/fixed-assets/page.tsx:507-513) whose per-asset errors are discarded at page.tsx:503.
verification.probe: Drove routers.fixed_assets.post_depreciation against the FakeDB from tests/test_r232_fixed_asset_depreciation.py (Rs 1,00,000 asset, WDV 24%, bought 2026-04-10), posting 2026-04..08, then 2026-10, then 2026-09. Printed: 2026-04 Rs 1,400.00 (pro-rated 21/30 days); 2026-05..08 Rs 2,000.00 each; 2026-10 Rs 2,000.00 (ONE month, September silently skipped, no warning); 2026-09 -> HTTP 409 'Depreciation already posted through 2026-10'. Final register state: accum Rs 11,400, posted_through 2026-10 — one month permanently missing.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed, and demonstrated by running it. routers/fixed_assets.py:302 `monthly = math.floor(Decimal(annual) / Decimal(12))` charges exactly one month per call; the only loop over periods is absent. routers/fixed_assets.py:279 is the high-water-mark guard `if asset.get('depreciation_posted_through') and asset['depreciation_posted_through'] >= period: raise HTTPException(409, ...)` — a lexicographic 'YYYY-MM' compare, so once a later month is posted every earlier one is refused permanently. The route table confirms there is no range/annual endpoint: the module exposes only GET '' (164), POST '' (187), POST /{asset_id}/depreciate (245), PATCH /{asset_id}/dispose (340), GET /depreciation-schedule (438). `grep -rn 'deprec' apps/api/jobs/` returns nothing, so no scheduler sweep. A Partner could post a manual journal for the missed month via POST /api/accounting/journal, but that touches the GL only — it never updates fixed_assets.accumulated_depreciation_paise or depreciation_posted_through, so the register and the ledger then disagree (and the year-end note's tie-out at routers/year_end_notes.py:337-373 would report the difference without saying which side is right). findings.title: The auto-generated Fixed Assets note reports a theoretical annual charge that need not match anything posted to the P&L
findings.evidence: routers/year_end_notes.py:76-110 `_compute_fixed_assets_note_data`: `gross_block` and `accumulated_dep` are summed from the register rows, but `dep_charge` is `sum(_annual_depreciation_for_period(a, fy_end_month))` — the theoretical full-year charge for every asset, regardless of how many months were actually posted, and with no pro-rata for an asset bought mid-year (the pro-rata at routers/fixed_assets.py:143-155 only ever applies inside `post_depreciation`). The note also filters `.eq("is_disposed", False)` (line 93), so an asset sold during the year disappears from gross block entirely instead of appearing as a deduction, and there are no additions/deductions columns at all.
findings.ca_experience: The Fixed Assets note in the signed financial statements shows a depreciation charge that does not equal the Depreciation Expense line in the P&L it is a note to — over-stated if months were missed (see FA-04), and always over-stated in the year of purchase. The Schedule III movement disclosure (opening gross block + additions − deductions = closing, same for depreciation) simply is not produced, so the CA has to rebuild the whole schedule by hand.
findings.market_standard: The Schedule III fixed-asset note is the standard output of any FA register: gross block opening/additions/deductions/closing and the same four for depreciation, per class, with the charge equal to what was posted.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute the charge from the GL (the depreciation journals whose entry_date falls in the FY) rather than re-deriving it, include disposed-in-year assets as deductions, and emit the five-column movement table per asset class.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The auto-generated Fixed Assets note's depreciation charge is the theoretical full-year figure summed from the register (routers/year_end_notes.py:97-100), not what was posted to the P&L: it ignores missed months (FA-04) and applies no pro-rata in the year of purchase, and it is printed into the Notes and Complete Pack PDFs by services/year_end_pdf_service.py:510-522. The note also produces no Schedule III movement table (only four closing figures at routers/year_end_notes.py:104-108). The net block IS tied out to the balance sheet (routers/year_end_notes.py:337-391); the depreciation charge is tied to nothing.

lens_notes.literal: Mostly confirmed, with one sub-claim corrected. routers/year_end_notes.py:76-111 `_compute_fixed_assets_note_data` sums `gross_block` and `accumulated_dep` from the register rows (lines 101-102) but computes `dep_charge` by calling `_annual_depreciation_for_period(a, period)` per asset (lines 97-100) — the FULL theoretical annual charge, with no reference to how many months were actually posted and no pro-rata for a mid-year purchase (the pro-rata at routers/fixed_assets.py:148-156 is applied only to the monthly figure inside post_depreciation at line 305, never inside _annual_depreciation_for_period). The `.eq('is_disposed', False)` filter is at line 92 (cited as 93). There are indeed no additions/deductions columns — `note_data` carries only gross_block_paise, accumulated_dep_paise, net_block_paise and depreciation_charge_paise (lines 104-108). CORRECTION to one half of the evidence: excluding a disposed asset from CLOSING gross block is the correct Schedule III treatment, and it also keeps the note tying to the ledger (the disposal journal credits the asset account by cost, services/phase2_journal_service.py:1307-1309). What is genuinely missing is the movement disclosure — opening + additions − deductions = closing, and the same four for depreciation — not the presence of disposed assets in the closing column.
lens_notes.guards: A partial one the finding did not mention, and it does not cover the defect. routers/year_end_notes.py:337-373 `_tie_to_balance_sheet` checks the note's NET BLOCK against tangible_assets + intangible_assets + capital_wip on the face of the Balance Sheet and, on a mismatch, `_tie_out_sentence` (375-391) writes 'THIS NOTE DOES NOT AGREE WITH THE BALANCE SHEET' into the note text. So an unposted or double-posted asset is caught. The DEPRECIATION CHARGE is tied to nothing — it is never compared with the Depreciation Expense line in the P&L — so the exact defect the finding names passes silently.
lens_notes.reach: Reachable and it reaches paper. Router mounted at main.py:348; the frontend calls the correct path `/api/year-end/${engagementId}/notes/generate` (apps/web/lib/api/yearEnd.ts:351-354) from the 'Auto-Generate All Notes' button (apps/web/app/clients/[id]/year-end/[engagementId]/notes/_page.tsx:87). The notes SCREEN renders only note.content, not note_data — but services/year_end_pdf_service.py:510-522 renders every `*_paise` int in note_data as a 'Particulars / Rs (Rupees)' table, so 'Depreciation Charge — Rs X' is printed in the Notes PDF and in the Complete Pack PDF (routers/year_end_exports.py:236-265, 282-323).

findings.title: IT Act §32 block-of-assets depreciation does not exist, and the book-to-tax bridge that needs it is dead code
findings.evidence: domain/income_tax/book_to_tax_bridge.py:18-38 states in its own docstring that §32 is 'per BLOCK OF ASSETS' and that 'NOTHING IN THIS CODEBASE IMPLEMENTS THE SECOND ONE'; `build_bridge` takes `depreciation_under_section_32_paise` as an Optional input and marks itself incomplete when absent (lines 88-135). Grep for `build_bridge` and `depreciation_under_section_32` across apps/api returns hits only in tests/test_book_to_tax_bridge.py — no router, no service imports it. Grep for 'deprec' in routers/income_tax.py, routers/itr_workspace.py and domain/income_tax/*.py returns only an XBRL tag name (domain/income_tax/xbrl_service.py:58). There is no block table, no 180-day half-rate rule, no §32(1)(iia) additional depreciation, no §50 short-term gain on a block, and no Form 3CD (grep for '3CD' finds only engagement-letter text).
findings.ca_experience: The single largest line in every Indian tax computation is missing. A CA cannot produce the depreciation chart (3CD clause 18), cannot compute taxable income for any client with assets, and cannot use this product for the tax side of an asset-holding client at all — which is the whole reason a CA firm buys ClearTax or Winman. Even the bridge that would flag the gap honestly is unreachable from any screen.
findings.market_standard: Winman and ClearTax both maintain the IT-Act block register alongside the Companies Act register: opening WDV per block, additions split by 180 days, additional depreciation, sale proceeds reduced from the block, §50 STCG when the block is exhausted, and the 3CD chart printed from it.
findings.suggested_fix: Build a block register (block key = rate class), driven by the same fixed_assets rows plus a block mapping, computing §32 depreciation per FY; then wire `build_bridge` behind an endpoint and a screen. This is the highest-leverage single item in the whole subsystem.

verification.what_is_actually_true: There is no IT Act §32 block-of-assets depreciation anywhere in apps/api — no block register, no 180-day rule, no additional depreciation, no §50 adjustment, no 3CD chart — and domain/income_tax/book_to_tax_bridge.py, the module whose docstring (lines 18-38) says so and which would mark the computation incomplete, is imported only by tests/test_book_to_tax_bridge.py and exposed by no router.
verification.probe: grep -rn 'build_bridge|depreciation_under_section_32' apps/api --include=*.py -> hits only in domain/income_tax/book_to_tax_bridge.py and tests/test_book_to_tax_bridge.py; grep -rni 'block.of.assets|block_of_assets' -> 1 hit (the docstring); grep -rn '3CD' -> 1 hit (routers/engagement_letters.py:224).

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed on every limb. domain/income_tax/book_to_tax_bridge.py:18-38 states in its own module docstring that §32 is 'per BLOCK OF ASSETS' and that 'NOTHING IN THIS CODEBASE IMPLEMENTS THE SECOND ONE'. `grep -rn 'build_bridge|depreciation_under_section_32' apps/api --include=*.py` returns hits only inside domain/income_tax/book_to_tax_bridge.py itself and tests/test_book_to_tax_bridge.py — no router, no service, no workspace imports it. `grep -rni 'block.of.assets|block_of_assets' apps/api --include=*.py` returns exactly one hit, the docstring line above. `grep -rni 'section_32|§32' apps/api --include=*.py` outside the bridge returns only routers/fixed_assets.py:149 and :304, both comments on the Schedule II pro-rata. `grep -rni 'deprec' routers/income_tax.py routers/itr_workspace.py domain/income_tax/` returns one hit, the XBRL tag name at domain/income_tax/xbrl_service.py:58. `grep -rn '3CD' apps/api --include=*.py` returns one hit, routers/engagement_letters.py:224, which is engagement-letter prose. ls domain/income_tax/ shows no block-register module. So: no block table, no 180-day half-rate split, no §32(1)(iia) additional depreciation, no §50 short-term gain on a block, no Form 3CD clause-18 chart.

There is no route anywhere whose path or handler mentions depreciation under the IT Act.

findings.title: Asset acquisition always credits Bank — no vendor, no GST/ITC, and no link to the purchase bill, so buying on credit double-counts the asset
findings.evidence: services/phase2_journal_service.py:1164-1215 `journal_for_asset_acquisition` posts exactly two lines: Dr <category account> cost, Cr `_find_account(..., "%Bank%", system_key="bank")`. models/accounting.py:149-160 `FixedAssetIn` has no vendor, payment-mode, GST or bill fields. routers/purchase_bills.py:1612-1627 routes goods lines only to `apply_purchase_to_inventory`; grep for 'fixed_asset' in routers/purchase_bills.py returns nothing, so a purchase bill can never capitalise into the FA register.
findings.ca_experience: Client buys a ₹5,90,000 machine (₹5,00,000 + 18% GST) on 30-day credit from a vendor. If the CA enters the vendor's bill as a purchase bill, the GL has Dr Plant & Machinery ₹5,00,000 / Dr GST Input ₹90,000 / Cr Creditor — but there is no asset in the register, so no depreciation is ever charged. If the CA then also adds the asset to the register to get depreciation, a second journal posts Dr Plant & Machinery ₹5,00,000 / Cr Bank — the asset is capitalised twice, bank is understated by ₹5,00,000, and the creditor is never cleared. There is no third option. Nothing in the product detects it (the reconciliation controls at services/reconciliation_service.py cover inventory, not fixed assets).
findings.market_standard: Zoho Books capitalises directly from the bill; Tally posts the asset ledger from the purchase voucher with the ITC split out. The register is a view of the ledger, never a second entry point that re-posts the same purchase.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the FA register capitalise FROM a purchase bill line (mirroring `apply_purchase_to_inventory`), or at minimum let `FixedAssetIn` carry a vendor/creditor or bill_id and an ITC-eligible tax split, and add a reconciliation check for 'asset in the register with no acquisition journal' and 'capitalised twice'.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Asset acquisition posts only Dr <category account> / Cr Bank (services/phase2_journal_service.py:1192-1207), FixedAssetIn has no vendor, bill or tax field (models/accounting.py:149-160), and routers/purchase_bills.py never capitalises into the register. A credit purchase entered as a bill against a fixed-asset expense_account_id and then also added to the register capitalises the asset twice with the creditor left standing, and no reconciliation check looks for it (services/reconciliation_service.py:518-527).

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed. services/phase2_journal_service.py:1164-1215 `journal_for_asset_acquisition` builds exactly two lines: Dr the category account resolved from `cat_map` (1180-1191) for the full `asset['purchase_cost_paise']`, Cr `self._find_account(db, firm_id, client_id, '%Bank%', system_key='bank')` (1192) for the same amount, narrated 'Bank payment for asset acquisition' (1205). findings.title: Disposal does not charge depreciation up to the disposal date, so the gain/loss on every mid-year sale is wrong
findings.evidence: routers/fixed_assets.py:341-437 `dispose_asset` reads the row, claims it, and computes `wdv = purchase_cost_paise − accumulated_depreciation_paise` (line 421) from whatever has been POSTED so far; there is no depreciation-to-date step. services/phase2_journal_service.py:1298-1320 uses the same stale `accum_depn` for the journal. The frontend shows the same figure to the CA before confirming (apps/web/app/clients/[id]/fixed-assets/page.tsx:770-780). There is also no output GST on the sale and no §50 block adjustment (see FA-06).
findings.ca_experience: An asset last depreciated to 31 August is sold on 15 January for ₹2,00,000. The four and a half months' depreciation the client is entitled to is never charged; WDV is overstated, so the loss on disposal is overstated (or a gain understated) by that amount, and the depreciation expense for the year is short. Both the P&L and the fixed-asset note are wrong, in a scenario every client has. On top of that the sale is a supply under GST and the journal credits the whole proceeds to Bank with no output-tax line, so GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B miss it unless the CA raises a separate invoice.
findings.market_standard: Every FA module runs depreciation to the disposal date as part of the disposal and shows the CA the split (charge to date, then gain/loss on the resulting WDV). GST on sale of a capital asset is raised as a tax invoice from the same action.
findings.suggested_fix: Inside `dispose_asset`, post the outstanding depreciation from `depreciation_posted_through` to the disposal month (pro-rated on days for the part month, reusing `_prorate_purchase_month`'s shape) BEFORE computing gain/loss, and show both figures in the confirmation panel. Add a GST-on-disposal path or, at minimum, refuse silently posting a disposal with proceeds and no tax treatment recorded.

findings.title: The year-end Fixed Assets schedule sums only journal lines dated inside the FY, so prior years' gross block vanishes

No opening balance is added. Fixed assets are balance-sheet accounts, so this yields the year's MOVEMENT, presented as the fixed-asset schedule.
findings.ca_experience: A client bought a ₹40 lakh machine three years ago and nothing since. The FY 2026-27 fixed-assets schedule shows ₹0 gross block and a total of ₹0 — while the balance sheet correctly shows ₹40 lakh. The CA sees an empty schedule for a client that plainly has assets and cannot tell whether that is a data problem or a software one. The mock branch above it (lines 288-298) returns a plausible-looking ₹80,000 Plant & Machinery row with gross/accum/net keys the live path never produces, so the two shapes do not even match.
findings.market_standard: A schedule to a balance-sheet caption is always the closing balance (opening + movement), and its line shape is identical whether it comes from demo data or the ledger.
findings.suggested_fix: For balance-sheet schedule types, sum all posted lines up to fy_end (or read account_period_balances, which the reporting rule in CLAUDE.md already requires) rather than only lines inside the FY window; and make the mock shape identical to the live one.

findings.market_standard: Zoho Books and every FA tool allow editing an asset before/after depreciation with an automatic recompute-and-reverse of the affected postings, or an explicit 'revise' entry.

findings.title: No CWIP, revaluation, impairment, component accounting, shift working, transfers or physical verification
findings.evidence: Grep across apps/api and apps/web for 'revaluation|impairment|component accounting|shift working|double shift|triple shift' returns only FX revaluation (services/fx_reporting_service.py), one policy-note string ('Impairment of assets', routers/year_end_notes.py:152) and one Schedule III caption/XBRL tag for Capital Work in Progress (services/year_end_pdf_service.py:313, domain/income_tax/xbrl_service.py:41). migrations/025_fixed_assets.sql defines the whole table: there is no CWIP flag, no revalued-cost column, no impairment column, no component parent/child, no shift factor, no transfer or verification history — `location` (migrations/054:89) is a single free-text field with no log.
findings.ca_experience: A manufacturing client under construction has nothing to put its CWIP in; a company that revalues land cannot record it; AS 28 impairment cannot be booked through the register; Schedule II Part A para 4 component accounting (mandatory where a component's cost is significant and its life differs) is impossible; extra-shift depreciation (Part C note 6: +50% for double shift, +100% for triple) cannot be applied even though it is routine for factories. Physical verification of assets — an audit requirement the CA performs every year — has no working paper here.
findings.market_standard: Tally famously has NO fixed-asset register, which is the opportunity the owner should be attacking. But the dedicated Schedule II tools CAs buy alongside Tally all do CWIP, revaluation, impairment, component split and shift working, because those are exactly why they are bought.
findings.suggested_fix: Sequence: CWIP + capitalisation-on-commissioning first (it blocks a whole client type), then shift working (a rate multiplier, cheap), then component accounting (a parent/child on the same table), then revaluation/impairment as value-only movements posted through the kernel.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The register genuinely has no CWIP, revaluation, impairment, component-grouping, shift-factor, transfer or verification columns (migrations/025 + 054:85-90 + 239 are the whole schema; routers/fixed_assets.py:64-95 is the whole depreciation computation), but 'nothing to put its CWIP in' and 'component accounting is impossible' overstate it — capital_wip is a mappable Schedule III schedule_line (routers/year_end_mappings.py:132) and components can be registered as separate asset rows. The repo-wide grep is as reported: revaluation hits are FX only (services/fx_reporting_service.py, migrations/149), impairment is one CA-input placeholder string (routers/year_end_notes.py:152), CWIP is a Schedule III caption (services/year_end_pdf_service.py:313, routers/year_end_mappings.py:132). apps/web/app/clients/[id]/fixed-assets/page.tsx:28,163,294,394 confirms location is one free-text box with no history.

findings.title: There is no closing-stock-as-at-a-date figure, and the date-filtered stock ledger's running balance does not foot
findings.evidence: domain/inventory_service.py:153-171 `_last_ledger_row` deliberately chains running totals by INSERTION order (`.order("created_at", desc=True)`), documented at length as the right call for backdated documents. findings.suggested_fix: Add an as-of-date valuation: either recompute the running columns for display in the requested order, or add a period-bucketed stock balance table maintained by trigger (the `account_period_balances` pattern CLAUDE.md already blesses). Surface it as a Stock Summary report with a date, and use it for the year-end tie-out to the Inventory GL account.

findings.title: Moving average is the only costing method — no FIFO and no standard cost
findings.evidence: domain/inventory_service.py module docstring lines 1-10 and `_compute_stock_in`/`_compute_stock_out` (lines 50-151) implement moving average and nothing else; the docstring says explicitly 'this is the defining trait of moving-average costing versus FIFO/LIFO, which track cost by batch instead'. migrations/188_inventory_costing.sql adds only `avg_cost_paise` to service_catalogue — there is no per-batch cost layer table, and no per-item valuation-method column anywhere.
findings.ca_experience: AS-2 and ICDS-II both permit FIFO or weighted average, and the client's chosen method is a disclosed accounting policy. A CA whose client's books are on FIFO — very common for traders in goods with volatile prices, and mandatory in substance for anything with batch/expiry — cannot migrate that client onto this product at all, because the closing stock value would change. There is no per-item override, so it is all-or-nothing across the whole book.
findings.market_standard: Tally Prime offers Avg Cost, FIFO, LIFO, Last Purchase Cost, Standard Cost and more, selectable per stock item. Zoho Books offers FIFO and weighted average.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a per-item `valuation_method` and a FIFO cost-layer table consumed by `_compute_stock_out`; keep the existing moving-average path as the default and pin both with the same style of pure-math unit tests already in tests/test_inventory_service.py.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Moving average is the only method and there is no per-item override (domain/inventory_service.py:50-151; migration 188 adds no method column). But the consequence is friction for a client whose disclosed policy is FIFO, not a wrong number: weighted average is permitted by AS-2/ICDS-II and the year-end policy note states the basis truthfully from the engine (routers/year_end_notes.py:222-223, 291-294). That is an absent market-standard option, i.e. medium, not high.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed. domain/inventory_service.py:1-10 states moving average 'versus FIFO/LIFO, which track cost by batch instead'; _compute_stock_in (50-114) and _compute_stock_out (117-151) are the only costing paths and both are unconditional. migrations/188_inventory_costing.sql:31-35 adds only opening_qty_units/opening_cost_paise/stock_qty_units/avg_cost_paise. Repo-wide grep for 'fifo|lifo|standard cost|valuation_method' over apps/api and apps/web returns no costing code at all (only 'BOM' as byte-order-mark and 'reorder' as list-reordering).
lens_notes.guards: One real guard the finding misses, and it is what drops the severity: the basis is DISCLOSED honestly rather than misstated. routers/year_end_notes.py:132-134 explains that moving-average is 'a property of the engine', :222-223 sets inventory_valuation_basis = 'moving average' from the engine rather than from a CA-entered policy, and :291-294 writes the note as 'Inventories - valued on the moving average cost basis, which is how stock movements are costed in these books.' So the software never certifies a policy it does not follow. AS-2 para 21 and ICDS-II both permit weighted average, so the figure produced is a permitted figure, not a wrong one.
lens_notes.reach: Real - it is the only costing engine behind every sale, purchase, credit/debit note and opening balance.

findings.title: No batches/expiry, godowns, item groups, alternate units, reorder levels, BOM or stock transfers — the Tally feature set an SME trader buys inventory software for
findings.evidence: migrations/176_service_catalogue.sql:21-39 defines the item master: name, description, hsn_sac, gst_rate_bps, default_rate_paise, a single free-text `unit`, notes, is_active. migrations/188 adds only opening qty/cost and the running stock cache. There is no batch table, no godown/warehouse table, no group/category, no second UOM or conversion, no reorder_level, no BOM, and `inventory_stock_ledger.movement_type` (188, extended by 189 and 191) admits only opening/purchase/sale/reversals/returns/adjustment/nrv_writedown — no transfer and no manufacture/consume.
findings.ca_experience: A pharma or FMCG distributor client cannot be onboarded: batch and expiry are not optional for them, and neither is a second godown. A manufacturer cannot record a production run at all — no BOM, no raw-material consumption, no WIP. A trader who buys in cartons and sells in pieces has one free-text unit. Nobody gets a reorder alert. For the owner's stated goal of replacing Tally, this is the gap that decides it: these are not advanced Tally features, they are the ordinary ones.
findings.market_standard: Tally Prime: stock groups, categories, multiple godowns with transfers, batches with expiry and manufacturing date, alternate and compound units, price lists, BOM and job work, physical stock vouchers, movement analysis. Zoho Books: warehouses, serial/batch tracking, reorder points, composite items, price lists.
findings.suggested_fix: Pick the two that unlock client types rather than all of them: godowns (with a transfer movement type) and batches with expiry. Both are additive to the existing ledger — a godown_id and batch_id on inventory_stock_ledger with the running chain keyed per (item, godown) — and neither disturbs the costing engine.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Batches/expiry, godowns and transfers, alternate units, reorder levels and BOM are all absent, and inventory_stock_ledger's movement_type CHECK (migrations/191:10-16) forbids a transfer or a manufacture row outright. The 'no group/category' part is refuted - service_catalogue.category exists (migrations/180:31-32). Severity corrected to medium: this is an absent market-standard feature set on a deliberately narrow module (migrations/176:7-11, 188:1-8), not a wrong figure or a blocked statutory task.

BUT the claim 'no group/category' is wrong: migrations/180_product_service_master.sql:31-32 adds `category TEXT` ('optional, free-text grouping') to service_catalogue.

findings.market_standard: Tally has Stock Ageing Analysis and Movement Analysis as standard reports; Zoho Books has an inventory ageing summary. This is also the kind of report that makes analytics addictive, which is the owner's stated aim.
findings.suggested_fix: An ageing report keyed off inventory_stock_ledger stock-in rows net of consumption, plus a 'days since last movement' column on the stock register. The answer is one row per item, so it may be a row set, but it must aggregate server-side per the reporting rule.

findings.title: Inventory cost excludes freight and non-creditable GST — closing stock and COGS are understated
findings.evidence: domain/inventory_service.py:995-1000 in `apply_purchase_to_inventory` takes `cost_paise = int(line.get("taxable_amount_paise") or 0)` — the line's taxable value only. Nothing adds freight, insurance, customs duty, or the GST that is not creditable (a composition dealer, an exempt supplier, or a §17(5)-blocked input). There is no landed-cost or additional-cost-of-purchase mechanism anywhere: grep for 'landed' across apps/api returns nothing.
findings.ca_experience: An importer or a trader who pays ₹40,000 freight on a ₹10,00,000 consignment carries stock at ₹10,00,000 instead of ₹10,40,000. AS-2 para 6 requires cost to include duties and taxes not subsequently recoverable, plus transport and handling. Closing stock is understated, profit is understated, and the number the CA certifies is wrong. For an unregistered or composition client the whole GST on every purchase should be in stock cost and none of it is.
findings.market_standard: Tally's 'additional cost of purchase' apportions freight and other costs across the stock items on the voucher; Zoho Books has landed cost. Both are standard, not premium features.
findings.suggested_fix: Let a purchase bill carry apportionable additional costs (by value or by quantity) that feed `total_cost_paise` in `record_stock_in`; and where the bill's ITC is not eligible, add the tax to the stock cost rather than to GST Input.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Stock is valued at the purchase line's taxable value only (domain/inventory_service.py:1000). There is no landed-cost or apportionment mechanism anywhere, so inward freight, insurance and customs duty stay in expense and closing stock is understated against AS-2 para 6; and because all GST including itc_eligible=false tax is debited to GST Input (services/phase2_journal_service.py:656-676), blocked credit never joins stock cost either. Medium stands: material for an importer or a freight-heavy trader, and only crudely workaroundable by grossing up the line rate, which distorts the line's GST.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed at the line cited. domain/inventory_service.py:1000 is exactly `cost_paise = int(line.get("taxable_amount_paise") or 0)`, and that is the only value passed to record_stock_in (:1002-1006), so stock cost is the line's taxable value and nothing else. The non-creditable-GST half is confirmed one level down: services/phase2_journal_service.py:656-676 debits GST Input with the bill's WHOLE cgst/sgst/igst regardless of purchase_bill_lines.itc_eligible (migration 240:29-30), so blocked s.17(5) tax never reaches the expense account either, let alone stock. Repo-wide grep for 'landed|freight|carriage|additional cost' over apps/api and apps/web returns nothing.
lens_notes.guards: One partial workaround, and it is not clean: a CA can gross the item's rate up to include inward freight, but that inflates taxable_amount_paise and therefore the GST on the line, and freight billed by a different transporter cannot go on the vendor's bill at all. Nothing validates or flags the omission. No test asserts AS-2 para 6 cost composition.
lens_notes.reach: Real - apply_purchase_to_inventory is the ordinary posting path for every purchase bill carrying a service_catalogue_id line.

findings.title: A §17(5)(h) ITC reversal on a stock write-off is posted to the GL but can never reach GSTR-3B Table 4(B)(1)
findings.evidence: domain/inventory_service.py:1522-1533 posts the reversal as Dr write-off account / Cr GST Input, citing §17(5)(h). services/gst_return_service.py:741-769 builds Table 4(B): the non-reclaimable list is built ONLY from `_bills_cancelled_in(...)`, and the reclaimable list from `itc_register_service.for_period`. migrations/285_*.sql:55-58 constrains `itc_reversal_register.reason_code` to reclaimable grounds ('rule_37','rule_37a',...), and services/itc_register_service.py:138-141 rejects anything not in RECLAIMABLE_REASONS. So there is no route by which a write-off reversal is declared on the return.
findings.ca_experience: The CA writes off ₹2,00,000 of damaged stock and ticks 'reverse ITC'. The books show the ₹36,000 credit reversed. GSTR-3B Table 4(B)(1) shows nothing, so the return claims credit the books have already given back — an under-declared reversal, which is exactly the mismatch the electronic credit reversal statement is designed to surface. The books-vs-return reconciliation in the same service will flag a permanent unexplained difference.
findings.market_standard: ClearTax and the GST-focused tools carry a reversal register covering the §17(5) grounds and feed 4(B)(1) from it.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the register's reason_code CHECK to permanent grounds (17_5_h at minimum), let the register hold `reclaimable=false` rows, and have `apply_stock_adjustment` record its reversal there so it flows into 4(B)(1). Note the code already warns (domain/inventory_service.py:1499-1505) that the amount is an approximation from the item's own gst_rate_bps — the register row should carry that caveat to the CA.

verification.what_is_actually_true: A CA who ticks 'reverse ITC' on a damage/theft/destruction write-down gets the s.17(5)(h) reversal on the GL (domain/inventory_service.py:1526-1531) and nothing in GSTR-3B Table 4(B)(1), because 4(B)(1) is built from cancelled bills and blocked-credit bill columns only (services/gst_return_service.py:741-751; domain/gst/gstr3b_computer.py:668-671) and the reversal register refuses permanent grounds (migrations/285:55-58, services/itc_register_service.py:138-141). Raised to high: the prepared return over-claims credit the books have already given back, which is a wrong statutory figure on a return the CA files - mitigated only in that the books-vs-ledger comparator at gst_return_service.py:826-833 will show an unexplained difference.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed, with one refinement to the evidence. post_stock_writeoff_journal_entry (domain/inventory_service.py:1494-1533) posts Dr write-off / Cr GST Input citing s.17(5)(h) at :1526-1531. On the return side the non-reclaimable list is NOT built only from _bills_cancelled_in: services/gst_return_service.py:741-751 builds it from cancelled bills, and blocked s.17(5) credit on live bills reaches 4(B)(1) separately through the computer (domain/gst/gstr3b_computer.py:668-671, 486-489, detail rows at gst_return_service.py:554-580). Either way neither route can see a stock write-off. The register is closed to it: migrations/285:55-58 CHECKs reason_code IN ('rule_37','rule_37a','section_16_2b','section_16_2c','other') and services/itc_register_service.py:138-141 raises ITCRegisterError for any non-reclaimable ground, by design ('a permanent reversal ... is Table 4(B)(1) and is derived from the documents, not registered'). A write-off is not a document, so it falls through the gap between the two.
lens_notes.guards: One real guard, and the finding already predicts it: services/gst_return_service.py:807-833 nets only itc_rev_perm_* + itc_rev_temp_* off books_itc and compares against gl['itc_paise'], the actual net debit movement on GST Input - which the write-off's credit HAS reduced. So itc_matched goes false and the CA sees an unexplained books-vs-ledger difference of exactly the reversed amount. It surfaces the problem; it cannot fix it, and there is no override or manual 4(B) entry anywhere in gst_return_service.
lens_notes.reach: Real end to end. The adjustment path is mounted (apps/api/main.py:306), routers/inventory.py:147-205 takes reverse_itc, and the UI offers it with a suggested default per reason (apps/web/app/clients/[id]/inventory/page.tsx:74-82).

findings.title: Opening the Inventory tab walks the client's ENTIRE stock ledger
findings.evidence: routers/inventory.py:31-63 `_last_ledger_rows` pages `inventory_stock_ledger` newest-first in 1000-row pages, looping `while remaining` and only breaking on an empty or short page. `remaining` never empties when any item has no ledger rows at all — a newly created product, the common case — so the loop reads every movement row the client has ever had, on every page load. CLAUDE.md's rule is explicit: 'No report may fetch rows proportional to transaction volume', with the 54-second cash-flow measurement as the worked example, and apps/api runs in Singapore against Postgres in Mumbai.
findings.ca_experience: For a trading client with a few years of daily movements the stock register takes progressively longer to open and will eventually hit lib/api's 45-second abort, which is deliberately never retried — the CA gets 'Couldn't load the stock register' on a client whose data is fine.
findings.market_standard: n/a — this is an internal performance rule the codebase sets for itself and this call site breaks.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace with a SQL function returning one latest row per item (DISTINCT ON (service_catalogue_id) ... ORDER BY created_at DESC), or break the loop once a full page has yielded no new item. The answer is one row per item; the read should be too.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The loop does scan the entire client stock ledger whenever any catalogue good has no ledger row, which is the ordinary state of a just-created product - 26 cross-region round trips over 25,000 rows in the probe below, versus 1 when every item has history. It breaks CLAUDE.md's rule that no report may fetch rows proportional to transaction volume, and it contradicts its own docstring at routers/inventory.py:35-37. Medium is right: it degrades with ledger size toward the 45s abort but produces no wrong figure.
verification.probe: scratchpad/probe/inv07.py, calling routers.inventory._last_ledger_rows against a stub PostgREST client that counts round trips. Printed: 'items asked for: 6, found: 5 / PostgREST round trips: 26 (rows scanned: 25000 of 25000)' and 'same client, no brand-new item: round trips 1'.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed, and the function's own docstring is what it contradicts. routers/inventory.py:30-62: `while remaining:` with breaks only on an empty page (:52-53) or a short page (:59-60). remaining is seeded from every kind='good' catalogue row (:95) with no is_active filter, so one item that has never had a ledger row - a newly created product, an archived one that never transacted - keeps the loop going to the end of the table. The docstring at :35-37 claims it 'stops as soon as every item has been seen, rather than scanning the client's entire movement history', which is exactly what it fails to do in that case. The query is also not restricted to the item ids being sought, so every page is a full-width read of the client's ledger.
lens_notes.guards: None found. No test references _last_ledger_rows (grep over apps/api/tests is empty), there is no LIMIT or row cap, and the frontend has no pagination - apps/web/app/clients/[id]/inventory/page.tsx:110-125 loads the whole register on mount with no arguments but client_id. apps/web/lib/api/index.ts:358-362 confirms the 45-second abort, and :396-399 confirms retries were removed.
lens_notes.reach: Real. Router mounted at apps/api/main.py:306; the Inventory tab is in the client nav (apps/web/lib/workspace/ClientNavContext.tsx:70) and calls it in a useEffect on every visit.

Neither fixed_assets.py nor year_end_notes.py imports it. The frontend register tab, by contrast, DOES page (apps/web/.../fixed-assets/page.tsx:159 wraps the query in `selectAll`), so the two views of the same register disagree above 1000 rows.
findings.ca_experience: A manufacturer or a hotel with more than a thousand assets sees a correct gross block on the Register tab (paged) and a truncated one on the Depreciation and Reports tabs and in the year-end Fixed Assets note — with no error. The note then reports a gross block lower than the balance sheet and the tie-out fires for a reason nobody can find.
findings.market_standard: n/a — internal correctness.
findings.suggested_fix: Route all three reads through core/db_paging.

findings.title: WDV depreciation never ends: useful life is ignored for WDV and salvage defaults to zero, so an asset is written down forever
findings.evidence: routers/fixed_assets.py:88-96: the WDV branch uses only `wdv_rate_percent` and never reads `useful_life_years`; the terminal condition is `wdv_now <= salvage` (line 82) with `salvage = asset.get("salvage_value_paise", 0)`. models/accounting.py:155 defaults `salvage_value_paise` to 0 and apps/web/.../fixed-assets/page.tsx:328 defaults the form field to "0"; the form only shows the Useful Life input when the method is SL (line 431). Schedule II Part C's note caps residual at 5% of original cost and requires the asset to be depreciated over its useful life.
findings.ca_experience: A ₹1,00,000 computer on WDV at 31.67% with salvage 0 still carries ₹1,244 after fifteen years and never reaches zero — the register accumulates a tail of never-retired assets, and the charge in the later years bears no relation to Schedule II, which would have written it down to 5% residual by year three. If the CA does enter a useful life alongside WDV, it is silently ignored.
findings.market_standard: Schedule II tools take life + residual, derive the rate, and write off the remaining balance in the final year of the useful life.
findings.suggested_fix: Make useful life and residual % the inputs for BOTH methods (see FA-02), derive the WDV rate, and write off the residual balance in the last year of life. At minimum, collect useful_life_years for WDV too and stop charging once it is exhausted.

verification.what_is_actually_true: WDV depreciation has no useful-life terminal condition: routers/fixed_assets.py:91 uses only the rate, and the sole stop is `wdv_now <= salvage` (line 81) with salvage defaulting to 0 everywhere (models/accounting.py:155, page.tsx:325). The Add-Asset form does not even collect a life for WDV (page.tsx:363, 426-437), so Schedule II's requirement to write the asset down to residual over its useful life cannot be met. Corrected figure: ₹330.64 remains after 15 years on a ₹1,00,000 computer at 31.67%, not ₹1,244. Adjacent and corroborating (belongs to a different finding, flagged not claimed): the `_DEFAULT_WDV_RATES` table at routers/fixed_assets.py:40-50 is not a consistent Schedule II WDV set — 31.67% for computers is the 3-year STRAIGHT-LINE rate (95/3), while 5.00% for Building is a genuine 60-year WDV rate.
verification.probe: cd apps/api && venv/bin/python — simulated 20 years of _compute_annual_depreciation on a ₹1,00,000 WDV/31.67%/salvage-0 computer with monthly=floor(annual/12) posting: closing WDV Rs 31903.36 (yr 3), 2218.84 (yr 10), 330.64 (yr 15), 49.48 (yr 20). Never reaches 0.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed except for one arithmetic claim. routers/fixed_assets.py:85-93: the SL branch reads `useful_life_years`, the WDV branch (line 91) reads only `wdv_rate_percent` / `_DEFAULT_WDV_RATES` and never touches useful_life_years; the only terminal condition is `if wdv_now <= salvage: return 0` at line 81-82 with `salvage = asset.get("salvage_value_paise", 0)` at line 78. models/accounting.py:155 is `salvage_value_paise: int = 0`; apps/web/app/clients/[id]/fixed-assets/page.tsx:325 defaults the form field to "0"; page.tsx:426-437 shows the Useful Life input ONLY when the method is SL and page.tsx:363 sends `useful_life_years: form.depreciation_method === "SL" ? ... : undefined`, so a WDV asset can never carry a life at all. WRONG NUMBER IN THE FINDING: a ₹1,00,000 computer at 31.67% WDV with nil salvage carries ₹330.64 after fifteen years, not ₹1,244 (₹1,036 at year 12). The mechanism — an asymptote that never terminates — is exactly as described.
lens_notes.guards: None. migrations/025_fixed_assets.sql has no CHECK tying useful_life_years to WDV and no residual floor. tests/test_depreciation_engine.py tests salvage capping (test_wdv_stops_at_salvage, test_wdv_with_salvage_value) but nothing about useful life under WDV or a 5% residual floor. The only practical stop is that once the annual charge falls below 12 paise, `monthly = floor(annual/12)` is 0 and post_depreciation returns 'No depreciation to post' (routers/fixed_assets.py:311-312) — the asset just sits there below its notional residual forever.
lens_notes.reach: Live and default. depreciation_method defaults to WDV in models/accounting.py:157, in migration 025 (`DEFAULT 'WDV'`) and in the Add-Asset form (page.tsx:323), and the WDV radio is preselected. Every WDV asset created through the UI has salvage 0 and no life.

findings.title: An explicitly entered 0% rate or 0-year life is treated as 'not supplied' and silently replaced by a default
findings.evidence: routers/fixed_assets.py:91 `rate_value = asset.get("wdv_rate_percent") or _DEFAULT_WDV_RATES.get(...)` and line 89 `life = asset.get("useful_life_years") or 5` — Python `or` treats 0 and 0.0 as absent. Same pattern at line 215 in `create_asset`. Land happens to be safe only because `_DEFAULT_WDV_RATES["Land"]` is also 0.00 (line 48). Nothing anywhere refuses to depreciate a Land asset if the CA picks the SL method — `_compute_annual_depreciation`'s SL branch (lines 88-90) ignores the category entirely.
findings.ca_experience: A CA who deliberately sets 0% on a fully-written-down or non-depreciable asset in any category other than Land gets that category's default rate instead, and the asset keeps depreciating. A CA who picks SL with a 5-year life on a Land row depreciates land, which is never permitted.

verification.what_is_actually_true: 'Post All for Period' is an unbatched sequential loop (page.tsx:506-513) whose per-asset call swallows every failure (`catch { /* ignore */ }`, page.tsx:504). findings.title: Stock quantity is NUMERIC(10,3) with no unit conversion, so high-count or fine-grained items break
findings.evidence: migrations/188_inventory_costing.sql declares `quantity_delta`, `running_qty_units` and `stock_qty_units` as NUMERIC(10,3) — seven integer digits. models/inventory.py:34 types the adjustment quantity as a plain `float` with only a positivity validator; domain/inventory_service.py converts via `Decimal(str(quantity))` (line 1480), so a float carrying more than three decimals is rounded by Postgres on insert while Python's computed running total keeps the full precision.
findings.ca_experience: A client dealing in grams, or a high-volume component distributor, tops out at 9,999,999.999 units per item. And an API caller passing 1.23456 units gets a stock ledger whose running total and stored quantity disagree in the fourth decimal — small, but the register is meant to be exact.
findings.market_standard: Tally supports compound units (box of 12 pieces) and decimal places per unit, which is how this is normally solved rather than by widening one column.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate the request quantity to three decimals at the boundary (apps/web/lib/money/rupeeInput.ts already exports `parseQuantity` for exactly this, per CLAUDE.md), and revisit the column width alongside the alternate-units work in INV-03.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The schema really is NUMERIC(10,3) with no alternate/compound units (migrations/188_inventory_costing.sql:32,34,56,59) and the boundary really does not validate decimal places (models/inventory.py:34,44-49; the frontend's step="0.001" at inventory/page.tsx:474 is inert because there is no form submit). But the specific drift claimed is wrong: running_qty_units is the same NUMERIC(10,3) column and is re-read from the DB on every movement (domain/inventory_service.py:502,544), so the stored running total and the stored deltas do not disagree — what is inconsistent is only that value_delta_paise/unit_cost_paise are computed on the unrounded quantity (domain/inventory_service.py:80).

No local Postgres was available (connection refused on 127.0.0.1:5432) to run the cast directly.

lens_notes.literal: Half confirmed, half wrong. Confirmed: migrations/188_inventory_costing.sql:32,34,56,59 declare opening_qty_units, stock_qty_units, quantity_delta and running_qty_units all NUMERIC(10,3) — max 9,999,999.999; models/inventory.py:34 types `quantity: float` and its only validator (lines 44-49) is `v > 0`; there is no alternate/compound-unit support anywhere (grep for alternate_unit/conversion_factor/secondary_unit over migrations, domain and models returns nothing — service_catalogue carries one free-text `unit`). REFUTED: the claimed running-total divergence does not occur. running_qty_units is stored in the SAME NUMERIC(10,3) column as quantity_delta, and every movement re-reads the previous total FROM THE DATABASE — `prev_qty = Decimal(str(prev['running_qty_units']))` at domain/inventory_service.py:502 (stock-in) and :544 (stock-out) — so the Python figure never 'keeps the full precision' across movements. Since the previous total is already exactly 3dp, round(prev + q) == prev + round(q) under Postgres's half-away-from-zero numeric rounding, so the stored chain stays internally consistent and check_inventory_cache_drift (services/reconciliation_service.py:228-287) compares two values that both came back from the same rounded columns.

maturity.rationale: Two very different halves. INVENTORY is a genuinely well-built perpetual moving-average engine: exact-total averaging that never drifts, a force-close invariant so an oversold item cannot leave phantom value, a documented oversold COGS true-up modelled on how QuickBooks and Dynamics handle it, a compare-and-set concurrency guard, one combined journal per document to dodge the idempotency trap, an NRV write-down citing AS-2/ICDS-II, a §17(5)(h) ITC decision the CA must confirm rather than have inferred, and three standing reconciliation controls that caught a real ₹38.14L drift. It is thinly FEATURED — moving average only, no batches, godowns, groups, alternate units, BOM, ageing or as-at-date valuation — but what exists is correct and tested (roughly 60 tests in tests/test_inventory_service.py alone). FIXED ASSETS is the opposite: 487 lines of business logic living in a router, with the arithmetic duplicated a third time in TypeScript. Its default 'Schedule II' rates are not Schedule II rates; monthly posting appears to fail outright in production because a 'YYYY-MM' string is written into a DATE column; disposal ignores depreciation to the disposal date; acquisition always credits Bank so a credit purchase double-counts; there is no edit path, no CWIP, no revaluation, no impairment, no component accounting, no shift working; and the entire IT Act §32 block regime — the thing a CA actually needs for the return — is absent, with the book-to-tax bridge that would consume it sitting unreferenced by any router or screen. The subsystem tells the CA it is doing Schedule II and it is not.
maturity.would_a_ca_buy_this_module_alone: Not yet — inventory is close to sellable to a simple trader but cannot value stock as at a date, and fixed assets would give a CA a wrong depreciation number on the first asset they enter while offering nothing at all for the tax computation.

open_questions_for_owner: Fixed assets vs Tally: Tally has NO fixed-asset register, so a correct Schedule II + IT Act §32 module is arguably the strongest single wedge this product has against the incumbent. Do you want to invest in making it best-in-class (blocks, 3CD chart, CWIP, component accounting), or keep it as a supporting register and put the effort into inventory instead? The two answers lead to completely different roadmaps.

Which client profiles must inventory serve in the next 12 months? Batches/expiry (pharma, food), godowns (multi-location traders) and BOM (manufacturers) are each a different multi-week build. Today the module fits a single-location trader on weighted average and nobody else.

Is FIFO a hard requirement? AS-2 permits weighted average, so a client already on weighted average migrates cleanly — but a client on FIFO cannot move without changing a disclosed accounting policy. How many of your target clients are on FIFO?

How is depreciation actually run in your target firms — monthly with the books, or once at year end? The current design assumes monthly and silently under-charges by 11/12 if a CA posts only March. If year-end is the real pattern, the run should be annual-first.

When an asset is bought, do you want the purchase bill to be the single entry point (bill line flagged as capital → asset created), or the register to stay a separate entry with a vendor field? Both are defensible; today neither is implemented and the two paths double-count.

Should the frontend keep its own copy of any statutory table? The WDV rate table exists in both routers/fixed_assets.py and the React page, and the annual-depreciation calculation exists in both places with different answers. Confirming 'never' would let this be fixed once rather than argued each time.

On FA-01 (the YYYY-MM into a DATE column): can you confirm from the live database whether any client has ever successfully posted depreciation? That single query tells us whether this is a latent bug or one that has been silently blocking the module in production since migration 054.
Rule 43 capital-goods ITC and GST on the sale of a capital asset both sit on the boundary between this module and GST. Do you want them owned here (with the asset) or there (with the return)?
strengths: The moving-average costing engine is the strongest thing in this subsystem. domain/inventory_service.py:50-151 computes the new average from the exact total cost in, never from a rounded unit cost, and `_compute_stock_out` force-closes the running value to exactly zero when quantity is exhausted so a long tail of small sales can never leave phantom value hanging off a zero balance — with the reason written beside the code.

The oversold true-up (domain/inventory_service.py:58-113, apply_purchase_to_inventory:1013-1022, post_inventory_trueup_journal_entry:757-820) splits a replenishing purchase between real on-hand value and a Dr COGS correction of the earlier sale that was priced at ₹0. That is the same mechanism QuickBooks and Dynamics use, implemented deliberately and tested (tests/test_inventory_service.py:58-103, 561-624).

Concurrency on the stock ledger is handled properly: `_insert_and_cache` (domain/inventory_service.py:216-282) compare-and-sets an integer `stock_version` — explicitly NOT the NUMERIC quantity, because that round-trips through Postgres in a different string form — before appending the ledger row, with a bounded retry (`_with_stock_cas_retry`, lines 195-214).

One journal per document, not per line: apply_sale_to_inventory:940-963 and post_inventory_receipt_journal_entry:692-756 both explain that per-line journals would collide with `_create_journal`'s (firm, client, reference_no, entry_date) idempotency guard and silently drop lines 2+ from the GL. That is a subtle trap seen and closed.

Three standing reconciliation controls for inventory — missing COGS journal, missing inventory-receipt journal, and cache-vs-ledger drift (services/reconciliation_service.py:160-240+) — each naming the exact invoice, bill or item. The cache-drift check exists because a real ₹38.14L drift was found and corrected by hand on 2026-07-25, and it is documented as such.

The opening-stock journal carries a hard-won bug fix in its docstring (domain/inventory_service.py:821-870): source_type is deliberately NOT 'Opening' because opening_balance_service's delta planner would otherwise zero out or double-post the Inventory account — 'Confirmed live'. That is exactly the kind of institutional memory a product this size needs.

The NRV write-down (domain/inventory_service.py:1641-1768, routers/inventory.py:203-258) is a value-only movement citing AS-2 / Ind AS 2 / ICDS-II, with its own movement_type (migration 191) and a no-op when NRV is already at or above cost.

The §17(5)(h) ITC reversal on a stock write-off is never inferred. models/inventory.py's docstring and the reason taxonomy in apps/web/app/clients/[id]/inventory/page.tsx:71-79 suggest a default per reason and always send the CA's confirmed value; routers/inventory.py:157-161 rejects reverse_itc on an increase.

Every inventory and fixed-asset write validates the period lock through `period_validation_service.validate_posting_date` — routers/inventory.py:174 and 240, routers/fixed_assets.py:201, 297 and 371 — and the fixed-asset ones carry the #232 note recording that this router previously checked nothing.

Disposal atomicity is done right: routers/fixed_assets.py:341-437 claims the asset with a conditional update (WHERE is_disposed = false) BEFORE any journal is posted, rolls the claim back on failure or a None journal, and is covered by six tests in tests/test_fixed_asset_disposal.py including the retry and double-submit cases.

The year-end Fixed Assets note ties itself out against the GL and says so in words — routers/year_end_notes.py:411-446 with tests/test_notes_tie_to_the_balance_sheet.py:116-137 asserting both the 'agrees with' and 'DOES NOT AGREE' outputs, plus a guard test that any future figure-bearing auto note must carry a tie-out.

Two IDOR classes were found and closed with the reasoning left in place: routers/fixed_assets.py:443-451 (cross-firm read of another firm's register) and 273-278 / 355-359 (row-addressed writes with no client scope), the latter reusing the 404 so the response is not an existence oracle.

The frontend distinguishes 'failed to load' from 'genuinely empty' everywhere in both pages (the M17 comments at apps/web/.../fixed-assets/page.tsx:146-149, 465-469, 810-813 and .../inventory/page.tsx:99-102) — so a timed-out request never renders as ₹0 gross block or an empty stock register.

Money discipline holds throughout: integer paise everywhere, Decimal rather than float in `_compute_annual_depreciation` (routers/fixed_assets.py:88-96), `_round_paise` with ROUND_HALF_UP in inventory, and both frontend forms parse rupee input through lib/money/rupeeInput.ts rather than parseFloat.

A TEST THAT ASSERTS THE WRONG BEHAVIOUR: tests/test_depreciation_engine.py:185, 190-195 and 197-202 assert the default rates as statutory fact — `test_wdv_furniture_schedule_ii_rate` docstrings 'Furniture & Fixtures: Schedule II WDV rate = 10.00%' and asserts `_DEFAULT_WDV_RATES["Furniture & Fixtures"] == 10.00`; the same pattern for Computers at 31.67% and Vehicles at 25.89%. Schedule II Part C gives furniture a 10-YEAR LIFE, which at the 5% residual cap is a 25.89% WDV rate, not 10.00%. The test pins the wrong number in place and names the statute while doing it (see FA-02).

THE STRUCTURAL BLIND SPOT: the mock-mode fake Supabase (tests/test_r232_fixed_asset_depreciation.py:41-110 and its twins) is a plain dict store with no column types and no constraints, so FA-01 — a 'YYYY-MM' string written into a DATE column — passes every test in the suite and fails on the first real request. The repo already has the right instrument for this (`test_*_pg.py` against real Postgres 16, a required CI check) and fixed assets uses it only for RLS (test_r3_3_legacy_invoice_fixed_asset_rls_pg.py). One real-Postgres test that posts a month of depreciation end to end would have caught the most serious finding in this report.

FRONTEND: apps/web/scripts/ holds ~20 behavioural guard tests (the filing-demo kill switch, payroll money exactness, pagination honesty, loading flags). None covers fixed assets or inventory, which is why FA-03's divergent TypeScript depreciation calculation and FA-15's decorative FY picker are both live.
what_exists:
FIXED ASSETS. One router, routers/fixed_assets.py (487 lines), holds the entire module including its arithmetic — there is no domain/ or services/ layer for it. Five endpoints: GET /api/fixed-assets (register, with current_wdv_paise derived per read), POST (create + auto-post the acquisition journal), POST /{id}/depreciate (one month at a time), PATCH /{id}/dispose, and GET /depreciation-schedule (which no screen calls). Data lives in one table, public.fixed_assets (migration 025, extended by 054/093 for asset_code, location, current_wdv_paise, depreciation_posted_through, journal_entry_id, and by 239 for the FY-fixed depreciation base). Depreciation is SL ((cost−salvage)/life) or WDV (opening-of-FY WDV × rate), computed in Decimal, charged as annual/12 per month, pro-rated by days only in the purchase month. WDV rates come from a nine-entry `_DEFAULT_WDV_RATES` dict keyed by asset category — there is no Schedule II Part C useful-life table anywhere in the repo, and the CA effectively types (or accepts) a rate rather than a life. All three journals — acquisition, depreciation, disposal — go through services/phase2_journal_service.py:1164-1336 and therefore through the one posting kernel `_create_journal`. The year-end Fixed Assets note is auto-computed at routers/year_end_notes.py:76-110 and tied out against the GL. There is no IT Act §32 block register, no CWIP, no revaluation, no impairment, no component accounting, no shift working, no asset transfer or physical-verification history, and no edit or delete path. domain/income_tax/book_to_tax_bridge.py would consume a §32 figure but is referenced only by its own tests.

INVENTORY. domain/inventory_service.py (1,768 lines) is a perpetual moving-average costing engine over two tables: service_catalogue (goods carry opening qty/cost plus a cached stock_qty_units/avg_cost_paise, migration 188) and inventory_stock_ledger, an append-only movement log whose running qty/avg/value are stored on each row and chained from the previously INSERTED row (not the previous movement_date — deliberately, so backdated documents stay in the chain). routers/inventory.py exposes only four endpoints: the stock register, one item's movement ledger, a manual stock adjustment, and an NRV write-down. Every other movement is a side effect of another document: sales invoices (stock-out + one combined COGS journal), purchase bills (stock-in valued at the line's taxable amount + an Inventory-vs-expense reclassification journal, plus an oversold COGS true-up where applicable), credit and debit notes, cancellations (reversals at the current average), and opening balances (Dr Inventory / Cr Opening Balance Equity). Adjustments post a write-off (with an optional CA-confirmed §17(5)(h) ITC reversal) or a surplus to Miscellaneous Income. services/reconciliation_service.py carries three standing controls: missing COGS journal, missing inventory-receipt journal, and cache-vs-ledger drift. There is no FIFO or standard costing, no batches or expiry, no godowns, no item groups or categories, no alternate units, no reorder level, no BOM or manufacturing, no stock transfer, no ageing or movement analysis, and no valuation as at a date.

SCREENS. Two client-workspace pages, both in the nav (apps/web/lib/workspace/ClientNavContext.tsx:70, 73): /clients/[id]/fixed-assets (948 lines; Register / Depreciation / Disposal / Reports tabs, the register read straight from PostgREST and the rest through the API) and /clients/[id]/inventory (635 lines; stock register with a ledger drill-down, adjust and NRV write-down modals). /accounting/fixed-assets is a five-line redirect stub.
